# Label placement: the round-7 placers against the shipped page (2026-10-07)

**Builders must not read `dev/label-trials/`.** Every number below is generated by
`vs-production/analyse.js` into `vs-production/results.md`, from raw lines kept on jasmine under
`/home/haws/label-trials-work/vsprod/` (they reproduce exactly from the specs, so they are not
committed).

Tom, 2026-10-07: *"It looks like we have solved placement. All builders now converge much higher in
terms of how much we show. And their discoveries are somewhat surprising (grow, don't shrink; stop on
a clock, not on a count). We should write up the report on this compared to current production."*

## 1. What was measured

- **Production** is the SHA Tom last pulled, `9c71d54f`. **Master** is `8c88e689`. For each, a `git
  archive` of the commit with the bench's `extract.js`, `generator.js`, `contract.js` and
  `js/lpn-label-scene.js` copied in, as round 6 §2.8 did: the page itself (`js/looped-network.js` on
  the node DOM stub, solved by the vendored EPANET engine) lays out every view, and its layout is read
  off the page and replayed into the bench (`vs-production/replay.js`).
- **The same 64 scene sets as round 7's E1** (1,000 nodes; grid, tree, suburban, downtown; secret
  seeds 71-74; plain and bent-and-valved; 28 and 44 px), five zooms each, 320 views, scored by the
  same bench and judges' measures (`vs-production/score-one.js` is round 7's `score-one.js` less the
  count probe). **Production's scenes are identical to round 7's, label for label and row for row
  (320 of 320 views checked)**, so A7-D7's round-7 lines are compared with it directly.
- **Master's scenes differ in the text only**: master prints one more decimal on some values (Qb=4.2
  where production prints Qb=4) and its EPANET solve differs in the second decimal, so its labels are
  wider. To compare like with like, A7 was run again on master's own scenes (A7@mast).
- **Time** for production and master is the page's whole `refreshLabelText()` pass (label text and
  layout, over the whole network, on the stub), not `place()` alone. It overstates placement, but it
  is what a reader waits for on the page today.

- **The gap is widest where the map is crowded**: labels shown at the five zooms, 1x to 4x, are

  where there was room for them; the round-7 placers 4.7-7.1%.
- **Speed**: production's page pass took over a second on 218 of 320 views (R10 asks for one second);
  no round-7 view did. The comparison flatters the builders a little (the page time includes composing
  the label text), but the page lays out the whole network on every pass, which is the larger part.
- Production lays nearly every pipe label it shows along its pipe (95%, against 51-70% for the
  builders), because it shows so few: it hides the pipe labels that cannot lie along.

## 3. The two discoveries, with their evidence

### 3.1 Grow, do not shrink

**The rule.** Give every label a place in its smallest form (the last value in the user's drop
order) before any label gets a second value; then grow, a value at a time, in rounds. Production does
the opposite: every node label starts from its full content (`runLabelCollisionAvoidance()`, "EVERY
NODE LABEL STARTS FROM ITS FULL CONTENT") and the ones that do not fit shed a property and try again
(`shedNodeLabelsForCrowding()`).

**Evidence.**
- All four builders reached it independently (phase-1 summary, strategy 1).
- Switched off on the judges' 8 secret sets (round 7, H3), it cost A 8.8 labels per 100 asked for, B
  2.9 and D 3.0, on 8 of 8 sets each, **with values shown about unchanged** (-0.7 to +0.2). So growing
  buys labels without spending values.
- The plain search placing labels from an empty map showed 78% of labels in smallest-first order and
  70% when each label took as many values as it could in turn: eight points from the order alone
  (strategy catalogue, S11).
- **Why it surprises.** Shrinking looks safer: start from what the user asked for and give up only
  what you must. But a full label seated early takes ground that three smallest forms needed; the
  shrink never gets that ground back, because the label that took it already fits. Growing asks every
  label for its smallest claim first and spends the leftover ground on values.

### 3.2 Stop on a clock, not on a count

**The rule.** After the first pass, keep improving (rescue search, eviction, growth) until a time
bound (450-700 ms), and never cap the work by how many labels there are.

**Evidence.**
- Three of the four builders stop on a clock; the fourth (D) had a count cap in round 6 and replaced
  it. Switched back to its old count cap on the secret sets, D lost **10.5 labels and 6.3 values per
  100 asked for, on 8 of 8 sets**, the largest single ingredient anyone measured (H3).
- A count cap also hides labels by count, which R1's second half forbids (*"Never hide it because of
  how many labels are already showing"*). Under the clock, far labels revived beyond control flips were
  0.3-3.2%, all under 5% (H6).
- **The price, measured here for the first time (§4): a placer that stops on a clock is not a pure
  function of the view.** Given the same view twice it can answer differently, because it got
  further the second time or less far. Production, which runs every pass to completion, never does.

## 4. Stable modelling: how many labels move after a small edit or a pan

**The metric (new; `vs-production/stability.js`).** The bench's `extract.js` gained a stability
sequence (spec `stab`): at 1x and 2x, the view; the same view again (a **control**); one field
**edited** (the elevation of the node nearest the view centre retyped with an extra leading digit, so
its Z row is one character wider, with no re-solve, as with Recalculate off); the edit **undone**; and
the view **panned** by a tenth of the canvas width. The placer runs through them in order with `prev`,
as on the page. Between two consecutive views, over the labels requested in both and shown in either,
**the edited label itself left out**, a label **changed** if it appeared or vanished, showed other
rows, turned by more than half a degree, or moved more than 1 px against its own anchor (so the pan,
which carries every anchor, moves nothing by itself). Unlike the bench's churn, a change that shows
more still counts: this is what a reader sees move. 32 sets (four families, seeds 71-72, plain and
bent-and-valved, 28 and 44 px).

**Labels changed per 100 shown** (in brackets: labels changed per view; comparisons with nothing
changed):

| | control (same view again) | edit (and its undo) | pan (a tenth of the width) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **production** | **0.00** (0; 64 of 64 still) | **0.04** (0.1; 118 of 128 still) | **0.00** (0; 64 of 64 still) |
| A7 | 13.9 (91) | 2.5 (16) | 4.0 (23) |
| B7 | 13.5 (87) | 4.4 (28) | 7.2 (42) |
| C7 | 3.2 (20) | **0.6** (4; 48 of 128 still) | 5.9 (34) |
| D7 | 44.0 (293) | 19.6 (127) | 18.4 (109) |

**Production is perfectly stable, and the round-7 placers are not.** Production lays out the whole
network on every pass, in a fixed order, to completion, so the layout is a pure function of the
drawing (its own `label-stability-harness.js` holds this): a pan changes nothing, and an edit that
widens one label moves almost nothing else (a tenth of a label per edit). The round-7 placers lay out
only the window, against a clock, carrying the last view's spots: the same view twice changes 3 (C) to
44 (D) labels in 100; one edit moves 4 (C) to 127 (D) other labels; a 10% pan changes 4-18 in 100.

**Two causes, both nameable.**
- **The clock.** A second layout of the same view is a new race against the time bound. This is the
  price of §3.2.
- **The opening idle.** C and D lay out the first view in the 3000 ms opening idle, and every later
  view in 450-650 ms. On the control, D's second answer to the very same view showed fewer labels
  (1,034 then 934 on the suburban set at 1x): the opening view was laid out with six times the time.
  This is the cold-start defect round 7 recorded (2.8), seen from the stability side.
- **The window.** Panning changes which labels compete at the edges, and the placers re-seat to suit.
  Production avoids this only by laying out the whole network, which is why it is slow (§2).

**What it means.** On this measure production is the model to keep, and the speed phase is where the
builders can earn it: a placer that converges before its clock is deterministic (speed-phase plan, T1),
and one that lays out a zoom ladder of the whole network in idle time gets production's stillness on
a pan (P3). Tom has asked for no stillness rule, and none is proposed; this is reported, as churn is.

## 5. A white paper: where, and when

**Advice.** Publish, in two steps, **after round 8 fixes the room measure** (round 7 record 2.8, fixes
1-2), because the paper's central "room left" figure is overstated until then. First an **arXiv
preprint** (primary cs.CG, cross-listed cs.GR and cs.HC): free, fast, citable, and the right home for
a bench, a protocol and negative results. Then a peer-reviewed version at the **ICA Commission on
Generalisation and Multiple Representation workshop** (label placement is squarely in its scope, and it
takes short papers) or **Cartography and Geographic Information Science**, with a short practitioner
note to the water modelling community (**WDSA/CCWI conference**, and the **Open Water Analytics /
EPANET** forums), which is where the readers who label pipe networks are.

**Outline (not drafted).**
1. Introduction: labelling a pipe-network map at every zoom; why interactive network maps differ from
   point-feature labelling (leaders, pipe labels along pipes, drop order of values).
2. Related work: point-feature label placement (Christensen, Marks and Shieber 1995; Imhof 1975),
   production labellers (ESRI Maplex, QGIS PAL, MapLibre), particle-based labelling (Luboschik et al.
   2008), trellis strategies (Mote 2007).
3. The contract and the bench: a placer as a pure function of one view; N1-N5 as hard rules; scored
   costs; the scene generator (families, bends, valves, up to 20,000 nodes).
4. Method: clean-room builders, secret scenes, pre-registered hypotheses, ablations to replicate each
   claimed strategy.
5. Results: the recipe the builders converged on; the two discoveries (grow, not shrink; a clock, not
   a count); against a shipped labeller (this report, §2).
6. Stability: the edit and pan metric (§4) and the cost of a clock.
7. Measuring room: why a one-label-at-a-time measure overstates room, and the held-back and realizable
   measures.
8. Negative results: ranked wedges, bolt-on repair, longer leaders.
9. Threats to validity; the bench and data released under the GPL.

## 6. What could port to master's placer, and what it would buy

Master's placer is the pass chain in `js/looped-network.js` `runLabelCollisionAvoidance()` (calling
`placeStationedLabels()`, `rankNodeLabels()`, `Collide.placeLabelsFirstFit()`,
`shedNodeLabelsForCrowding()`, `Collide.placeLabels()`, `Collide.repairCrossingGangs()`,
`shedCrossingLabels()`, `yieldStationedLabels()`), with the candidate and index code in
`js/lpn-collide.js`. Gains are the round-7 ablations (labels per 100 asked for, secret sets); in
master's chain they would be smaller, since each was measured inside a placer that had the others.

| # | Rule | Where on master | Estimated gain | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | **First look at master's 204 pipe labels over node symbols** (a defect, not a port) | `placeStationedLabels()` / `staticObstacles()` | removes every plain-network overlap | low; a defect to file |
| 1 | **Clean ground first**: accept only crossing-free spots on every pass but the last | `Collide.placeLabelsFirstFit()` (a two-tier accept) | label on pipe: B7 5.9 per 100 against master's 32.3; costs a few labels | low; deterministic, local |
| 2 | **Dense rescue search** for a node label the first-fit dropped: rays every 15 degrees at every half row out to 3-4 rows | `Collide.candidatesFor()` / `rayCandidates()`, called for dropped labels after `placeLabelsFirstFit()` | +3 to +6 | low to medium; additive, costs time |
| 3 | **Eviction**: a dropped label may move one or two neighbours that still show | after `placeLabelsFirstFit()`, beside `repairCrossingGangs()`, which already re-places labels jointly | +0.5 to +7 | medium; must keep the pass a pure function (`node-yield-harness.js`) |
| 4 | **Grow, do not shrink** | replace `unshedNodeLabels()` + `shedNodeLabelsForCrowding()` with smallest-form first-fit, then growth rounds | +3 to +9, the largest | high: `shedAlignedForConflicts()` and `predictNodeLabelBoxes()` assume full content; every rung rebuilds glyphs in the DOM |
| 5 | **Lay out the window, not the network** | the `doc.nodes.forEach` / `doc.links.forEach` loops in `runLabelCollisionAvoidance()` | page pass from 1.6-3.8 s toward the builders' 0.1-0.7 s | high, and it costs production's pan stability (§4) |
| 6 | **A clock** | none | not recommended as a clock: it breaks master's pure-function invariant; port it as "converge, then stop", with the clock only a safety cap | |

**The clean way is not a transplant.** Rules 1-3 port cleanly one at a time. Rules 4-6 rewrite the
chain, and the plan of record already does that better: merge `feat/label-placer` (the `?placer=` seam,
`js/lpn-label-scene.js`) with the chosen placer. Nothing is ported yet.

## 7. Threats to validity

- The page's time includes composing the label text; `place()` alone would be faster.
- Master's scenes carry wider text, so master's own row in §2 mixes the placer with its formatting;
  A7@mast separates them.
- The stability metric uses one kind of edit (a wider Z row), one pan size and two zooms.
- The room measures keep the blind spots round 7 recorded (2.8).
- One shared machine; the clock placers would show fewer values, and change more, on a slower one.
